lesson.title: Which Function Wins in the Long Run?
lesson.summary: When two functions both grow without bound, the limit of their ratio reveals which one is truly winning the race to infinity, a question far more subtle than which one looks bigger at small values of x.
lesson.body:
Two different functions can each march off to infinity as x grows large, yet do so at wildly different speeds. To make "different speeds" precise, compare the limit of the ratio of two functions as x approaches infinity: lim as x approaches infinity of f(x)/g(x). If this limit equals 0, then g(x) eventually outpaces f(x), no matter how far behind g(x) started. If the limit equals infinity, then f(x) is the faster grower. If the limit equals some finite nonzero number, the two functions grow at comparable rates, differing only by that constant factor in the long run.

This idea builds directly on limits at infinity, since the comparison is nothing more than evaluating lim x to infinity of a quotient, and it requires knowing what exponential functions look like, since exponential growth turns out to be the fastest broad category of growth among ordinary functions. A helpful hierarchy, justified piece by piece in the sections that follow, is that logarithmic functions grow slower than any positive power of x, positive powers of x grow slower than exponential functions with base greater than 1, and within each category, higher degree or larger base eventually wins.

Compare f(x) = x^2 and g(x) = 2^x. At first glance x^2 looks competitive: at x=10, f(10)=100 while g(10)=1024, so the exponential is already ahead. Push further: at x=20, f(20)=400 while g(20)=1,048,576, and the ratio f(20)/g(20) is about 0.00038. At x=30, f(30)=900 while g(30)=1,073,741,824, and the ratio is roughly 0.0000008. The ratio is not just shrinking, it is collapsing toward 0 far faster than the numerator is growing, because every time x increases by 1, g(x) doubles while f(x) only grows by a modest additive amount near that scale. This numerical trend reflects the true limit, lim x to infinity of x^2/2^x = 0, so the exponential dominates the quadratic no matter how large the quadratic's head start looked at small x.

The middle case, where the ratio approaches a finite nonzero number, deserves its own quick illustration. Compare f(x) = 3x^2 and g(x) = 5x^2: the ratio f(x)/g(x) = 3x^2/5x^2 = 3/5 for every x other than 0, a constant that never changes as x grows. Both functions have the same degree, so neither is truly winning; they grow in lockstep, always maintaining the same proportional relationship no matter how large x becomes. This is why growth rate comparisons single out degree and base as the deciding factors, not the size of any individual coefficient standing in front of a term.

This is the essential lesson of comparing growth rates: initial size at small x says almost nothing about long run behavior. A function can be smaller everywhere on a huge initial stretch of the domain and still overtake its rival permanently once x is large enough, because its rate of growth compounds differently. The sections that follow pin down exactly how polynomial, exponential, and logarithmic functions compare to each other and to themselves, using this same ratio test as the underlying tool, and later sections use the same idea to identify the dominant term inside a single expression.
